notes: MD 2000 places the PDG in slot 1; as Bongo's ruling single party since March 1968 it must sit in ruling slot 0. Gabon has no real coalition partner, so coalition slot 13 holds the presidential/Haut-Ogooué power network inside the regime. Pre-1968 parties (UDSG, PUNGA) appear as banned legacy networks; Aubame is imprisoned.

0.name: Parti démocratique gabonais
0.text:
The PDG was founded on 12 March 1968 by President Albert-Bernard Bongo, who succeeded Léon M'ba in 1967 and then dissolved all other parties. It absorbed M'ba's Gabonese Democratic Bloc and is now the sole legal party, the framework of 'national renovation' under a young, energetic president.

The party preaches national unity above ethnic rivalry, a liberal economy driven by oil, manganese and timber, and an unbreakable alliance with France, whose troops and advisers guard the regime. Its power rests on state patronage, on French protection and on Bongo's skill at co-opting every potential rival into government.

1.name: Archidiocèse de Libreville
1.text:
The Catholic Church is Gabon's largest religious institution, running schools, missions and hospitals since the nineteenth century. In 1969 André-Fernand Anguilé became the first Gabonese Archbishop of Libreville, symbolising the Church's transition to African leadership.

The Church supports social stability, Christian education, family values and the Western orientation of the state, while its clergy occasionally voice concern about corruption and authoritarian excess. Its leverage lies in the schools that train the Gabonese elite and in a large, devout following across the Estuary, Woleu-Ntem and Ogooué provinces.

2.name: Union démocratique et sociale gabonaise
2.text:
The UDSG was the main rival of M'ba's party, led by Jean-Hilaire Aubame, the Fang former deputy in the French National Assembly. After the February 1964 coup briefly made Aubame head of government, French paratroopers restored M'ba, and Aubame has been in prison ever since; his party is banned.

Aubame's followers stand for multiparty democracy, a free press, constitutional limits on presidential power and a fairer share for the Fang north. They accept the Western alliance but resent French interference. Their leverage lies in the Woleu-Ntem and among Libreville's educated Fang, who regard Aubame as a martyr.

3.name: Parti de l'unité nationale gabonaise
3.text:
PUNGA was founded in 1958 by René-Paul Sousatte and other radical intellectuals who campaigned for a 'no' vote in de Gaulle's referendum and for full independence. Dissolved since the advent of the single party, it survives as a loose network of teachers, clerks and former trade unionists.

Its heirs favour social reform, labour rights, public education and a fairer distribution of oil and manganese revenues, within a democratic and less French-dependent state. Their leverage is modest but real among Libreville's salaried workers and the educated young who feel excluded from the PDG's patronage system.

4.name: Le Cercle marxiste de Libreville
4.text:
A small, clandestine circle of young graduates returning from universities in France and the Soviet bloc meets in private homes in Libreville. Inspired by the revolution next door in Brazzaville, they read Lenin and study the Congolese Party of Labour as a model.

They call for nationalisation of oil, manganese and uranium, the expulsion of French troops and an alignment with the Soviet Union. Watched closely by the security services and French advisers, they have little reach, but their ideas spread among students and junior civil servants frustrated by the regime's dependence on France.

5.name: Association générale des étudiants gabonais
5.text:
The AGEG organises Gabonese students in France and is affiliated with the Federation of Black African Students in France. Radicalised by May 1968 and the anti-imperialist struggle, it is the loudest opposition voice the regime faces, issuing manifestos against Bongo and the French presence.

It denounces neocolonialism, the single party and the plunder of Gabon's resources by French companies, demanding democratic freedoms and a socialist revolution. Its leverage lies in its members, the country's future elite, whom the regime must either co-opt with posts or alienate by repression.

6.name: Les Héritiers d'Alar Ayong
6.text:
Alar Ayong, the Fang clan-regrouping movement of the late 1940s, sought to reunite the scattered Fang clans under their own customs and leaders. Its spirit lives on among elders of the Woleu-Ntem and the Ogooué valley who resent both French influence and the new Libreville elite.

The Heirs stand for Fang unity, customary law, clan authority and the rejection of Western lifestyles, foreign churches and the French grip on Gabon. They look sympathetically to anti-Western nationalism abroad. Their leverage lies in the village councils and clan networks of the north, Gabon's most populous region.

7.name: Le Comité révolutionnaire
7.text:
In February 1964 a group of junior officers calling themselves the Revolutionary Committee seized President M'ba, only to be crushed within two days by French paratroopers. The plotters were imprisoned or dispersed, but the memory of the coup lives on among young officers humiliated by French intervention.

They stand for a strong national state free of French tutelage, an army commanded by Gabonese and a tough line against corruption, open to partnership with non-Western powers. Their leverage lies in discontent within the junior ranks, which Bongo counters with promotions, French officers and a carefully selected presidential guard.

8.name: Les Négociants libanais de Port-Gentil
8.text:
Lebanese families, many of them Shia from South Lebanon, run shops, timber trading and import businesses in Port-Gentil and Libreville. Their notables follow the revival led by Imam Musa al-Sadr, who founded the Supreme Islamic Shia Council in Beirut in 1969.

They favour a modern, socially engaged Shia identity, community schools and good relations with the Gabonese government and French trading houses. Their influence lies in commerce and credit: Lebanese merchants dominate much of the retail and wholesale trade in the coastal towns, and they cultivate officials who can grant licences and concessions.

9.name: Le Cercle de Tyr
9.text:
Among the young Lebanese Shia of Libreville, a small devout circle formed around men educated in the religious schools of Tyre and in contact with the seminaries of Najaf. They meet for prayers and lectures in private homes and keep their distance from the community's wealthy notables.

They preach strict observance, the authority of senior clerics and the rejection of Western materialism, viewing Shia Islam as a complete social and political order. Their numbers are minimal, but they shape opinion within family networks and among poorer shop workers of the diaspora.

10.name: Les Imams de Libreville
10.text:
Gabon's Muslims are mostly West African traders and workers, Senegalese, Malian, Hausa and Beninese, settled in Libreville, Port-Gentil and the mining towns. Their imams and elders lead small mosques and act as intermediaries with the authorities.

They practise a conservative Maliki Sunni Islam, avoid political controversy and seek protection for their trade and worship from a government courting Arab oil states. Their leverage lies in commerce and in contacts with Saudi Arabia, Morocco and the Muslim World League, which offer funding for mosques and Qur'anic schools.

11.name: La Voie de Sokoto
11.text:
Among Hausa traders in Libreville and the timber camps, a small circle venerates the memory of the Sokoto Caliphate and Usman dan Fodio's jihad. It meets around itinerant preachers from northern Nigeria and Niger, outside the established mosques.

It preaches that Muslims must live under sharia and a caliph, condemning Western secularism, French influence and the compromises of established imams. It has no weapons and few followers, but its message finds an audience among young migrant workers who feel exploited and despised in a Christian-majority country.

12.name: Les Anciens d'Al-Azhar
12.text:
A handful of West African and Gabonese Muslims returned from studies at Al-Azhar in Cairo, where they encountered the ideas of the Muslim Brotherhood. They teach Arabic and religion in Libreville's Qur'anic schools and lead community associations.

They promote modern Islamic education, moral renewal, charitable welfare and an Islam engaged in public life, as an alternative to both Christian missions and Marxism. Their influence lies in teaching and associational life, and they hope that Gabon's growing ties with Arab oil states will open doors for Islam in public life.

13.name: Les Barons du Haut-Ogooué
13.text:
Behind the PDG stands the presidential system itself: a network of loyal ministers, prefects and administrators drawn heavily from Bongo's home province of Haut-Ogooué and from the Téké and Obamba peoples. They manage the oil and mining revenues that flow through the presidency.

The Barons prize stability, centralised power and the steady distribution of patronage, caring little for ideology or bloc politics. They favour pragmatic deals with any investor. Their leverage is immense: they control appointments, budgets and the security services, making them the true inner circle of the regime.

14.name: Bwiti
14.text:
Bwiti is a syncretic spiritual movement rooted in the Mitsogo and Fang traditions, using the sacred iboga plant in initiation rites and blending ancestral worship with Christian elements. Its chapels are found throughout Gabon, and many politicians, including the late Léon M'ba, have been initiates.

Bwiti defends ancestral customs, community solidarity and spiritual independence from both missionary churches and imported ideologies, maintaining a neutral stance in the Cold War. Its leverage lies in its vast following, especially in rural areas, and the respect its leaders command among elites who seek spiritual legitimacy.

15.name: Compagnie minière de l'Ogooué
15.text:
COMILOG, founded in 1953 by French and American steel interests, has exploited the huge manganese deposits at Moanda since 1962, exporting the ore by cableway and the Congo-Ocean railway. Together with Elf's oil operations at Port-Gentil and the uranium mines of Mounana, it forms the backbone of Gabon's economy.

The mining and oil companies favour stability, low taxes, French protection and a government that leaves extraction to foreign capital. Their leverage is decisive: they provide most of the state's export earnings and maintain close ties with the presidency and the French Africa networks.

16.name: Les Forestiers de l'Okoumé
16.text:
Gabon's timber trade is built on okoumé, the soft wood prized by the world's plywood industry. Alongside large French firms, a class of independent Gabonese and European loggers, sawmill owners and transporters works the forests of the Ogooué and the Estuary.

The Foresters want free access to concessions, lower export duties, less red tape and protection from the monopolies of large firms and state-linked companies. Their leverage lies in timber exports, still Gabon's main source of rural employment, and in close ties with local officials who allocate the forest permits.

17.name: Service des Eaux et Forêts
17.text:
The Water and Forests Service manages Gabon's vast rainforests, covering most of the country, and the Lopé wildlife reserve established in 1946. Its foresters, many trained in France, struggle to control the logging companies that strip the coastal forests of okoumé.

They advocate sustainable quotas, reforestation, protection of elephants, gorillas and chimpanzees and limits on hunting in the reserves. They have little political weight but hold technical authority over concessions, and their warnings about the exhaustion of the coastal forests give the government arguments for regulating the timber trade when it wishes.

18.name: Les Syndicalistes de Port-Gentil
18.text:
Port-Gentil, Gabon's oil and timber capital, has the country's largest concentration of wage workers: refinery hands, dockers, sawmill workers and oil drillers. Their union activists, absorbed into the PDG's controlled labour structures, still press for workers' interests behind the facade of national unity.

They demand higher wages, Gabonisation of skilled jobs held by Europeans, social housing and a larger share of oil revenues for the people. They favour a humanist African socialism over the Soviet model. Their leverage lies in strikes in the oil and timber sectors, which could quickly hit the state's revenues.

19.name: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
19.english: Federation of Black African Students in France
19.native_full: Fédération des étudiants d'Afrique noire en France
19.text:
FEANF, founded in 1950, unites African student associations in France and has long been the cradle of anti-colonial radicalism. By 1970 Maoist and other independent Marxist currents dominate its leadership, and Gabonese members are among its most active critics of the Libreville regime.

The federation denounces French neocolonialism, the African single-party regimes and Soviet revisionism alike, advocating a people's war and peasant mobilisation on the Chinese model. Its leverage lies in its intellectual influence on future African elites and in pamphlets that circulate secretly in Libreville's lycées.
19.wiki: Federation of Black African Students in France

20.name: Le Gabon aux Gabonais
20.text:
Since the 1962 riots that drove out thousands of Congolese, resentment against foreign Africans has been a recurring force in Gabonese politics. Clerks from Dahomey and Togo, traders from West Africa and Equatorial Guinean labourers are accused of taking jobs and wealth that should belong to Gabonese.

The movement demands the Gabonisation of jobs, restrictions on immigration, priority for nationals in trade and administration, and the expulsion of undesirable foreigners. It has no formal organisation but finds an echo in the PDG's youth wing and among the urban unemployed of Libreville, where a single incident can spark anti-foreign riots.

21.name: Les Affreux
21.text:
Libreville has served as a rear base for French mercenaries and arms flights to Biafra, and soldiers of fortune such as Bob Denard move freely through the capital under the protection of Jacques Foccart's networks. The Africans call them 'les Affreux', the Terrible Ones.

These hardened veterans of Katanga and Yemen embrace a violent anti-communism and a cult of force, serving as hired guards and instructors for Bongo's presidential security. They have no popular base, but their leverage is real: they are ready to fight any coup, revolution or communist incursion for the right price and the right patrons in Paris.

22.name: Forces armées gabonaises
22.text:
The Gabonese Armed Forces are small, French-trained and still partly commanded by French officers. Since the failed coup of 1964, the regime has kept them under tight watch, relying on the French marine battalion stationed at Camp de Gaulle in Libreville as the ultimate guarantor of power.

The officer corps values order, national unity and its own privileges, accepting civilian rule as long as its status is secure. It is divided between loyal officers rewarded by Bongo and younger men resentful of French command. Its leverage lies in its weapons and the latent threat of another putsch.

23.name: Les Rois de l'Estuaire
23.text:
The Mpongwe clans of the Gabon Estuary descend from the coastal kings who traded with Europeans for centuries, among them King Denis Rapontchombo, who signed the first treaties with France in the 1840s. Their chiefly lineages, together with the Orungu dynasty of Cape Lopez, still command respect.

They defend the dignity of the old coastal aristocracies, customary land rights in and around Libreville and Port-Gentil, and a role for chiefs in local affairs. Their leverage is symbolic and social: their lineages own valuable land in the capital, and the regime honours them to secure coastal loyalty.
